Now I've got the overall picture. The language is a simple scheme, equipped with quote, if, cond, let, define, set!, lambda, begin/progn, and general application. Primitives like display, newline, read, putchr, and the file operations fopen, fgetchr, fputchr, fdisplay, fread, and fclose are also in place. In the read test the input is "Reading" followed by a number, and calculator.scm reads a list and branches on the operator. For that reason my interpreter must also be able to read such lists.

The interpreter that will be written is, in short, to take one line from stdin as a file path, and to interpret the rest of the input as the input of that file. In order to redirect the rest of the input, a way to get the current position of the file object is necessary. Since the current position cannot be obtained with the given primitives, I intend to put in a helper called rest-of-input. This reads in one character at a time with getchr, and if it receives the end-of-file, stops and returns a string. If the input is empty, then by having it return the empty string, it will match the behavior of read at end of file.

With this the inner program can be made to read from that saved input, and the outer getchr and the inner one will no longer compete. Since the test files are self-contained the remaining input is nothing, but that is no problem.

The body of the interpreter will first parse the read input into a list of s-expressions and then evaluate them in order. The result of evaluation is not displayed, but side effects such as display will come out to the output. If an error occurs, then it will stop there and exit. In order to parse, since the inner interpreter needs its own parser, I will also put in a small read-from-string. This can also be used in a self-interpreting interpreter.

There are a few fine points to be careful of. Since the if condition is judged to be true as long as it is not the false value, I will follow the same policy. cond will treat a clause as applicable if the test is the else symbol or if the evaluation result is not false. When evaluating a function definition in the short form, the name of the function must also be bound to the new environment in which the body is to be executed. That is what makes recursion possible. In let as well, all the initial values are evaluated in the old environment, and the body is then executed in a new environment where the results are bound.

The representation of the environment will be as a list of pairs, and the lookup of a variable will be done by searching through it in order. The lookup of the primitive functions will be done by testing the name against a list. As for what the representation of a procedure is, that is something I have not yet fully decided. In any case I will now write out the file and try it out. If there are any problems I will discover them in the testing.
